text: A language model can do only one thing: given some text, produce the next token. Yet agents book meetings, run code and search the web. The trick is not inside the model at all; it is a loop around it, and once you see that loop clearly, both the power and the fragility of agents make sense.

When a model calls a tool, it writes text in an agreed format, for example a small block of JSON naming a function and its arguments, and then it stops. The program around the model, often called the harness, parses that text, checks it, runs the real function, and writes the result back into the context as new tokens. The model never touches the outside world. It only reads and writes, like a manager who passes written requests through a hatch and reads the replies that come back.

Models learn this format from training data. Toolformer, from Schick and colleagues at Meta, let a model insert candidate API calls into ordinary text and kept only the calls whose results made the following tokens easier to predict, so the model taught itself when a calculator or a search engine would help. Chat models are generally fine-tuned on many examples of tool calls written in their chat template, which is why they can produce well-formed calls when given a list of tool descriptions.

An agent is that exchange, repeated. In the pattern described by the ReAct paper, from Yao and colleagues, the model alternates between reasoning in text about what to do next, taking an action through a tool, and reading the observation that comes back, until it decides that it can answer. Each turn is appended to the context, so the agent's working memory is literally the growing transcript, and the KV cache from an earlier lesson can let each new step reuse the work already done on the earlier ones.

The same loop explains why agents fail. If each step goes right with some probability, the chance that a long chain of steps all go right shrinks multiplicatively. A step that succeeds nine times in ten gives a ten-step task only about a one in three chance of finishing cleanly, if the errors are independent. And errors feed forward, because a wrong observation becomes part of the context that every later step reads.

So a well-built harness adds structure. It validates arguments against a schema before running anything, returns clear error messages that the model can read and recover from, caps the number of steps, and asks for confirmation before actions that cannot be undone. Each of these turns a silent failure into text that the model, or a person, can act on.

Tools and agents do not change what the model is, a predictor of the next token; they change what its tokens are connected to. That raises a hard question: how do you know whether any of it is working? The next lesson, on evaluating models, takes that question seriously.
